nodes.body: It is the end-of-season sale at the Blue Lock boatyard. Three tables of other people's things stand in the grey rain. You look through a box of old bits: rusty tools, brass rings, and a single stiff leather glove. You spot a chipped enamel compass. It is dull yellow around the rim. Scratched into the back, so faint you can only see it when you tilt it, is a row of six small marks. A wavy line runs under them.

choices.label: Open the compass case and read the card tucked inside.

nodes.body: Inside the case is a card folded eight times. It is as soft as cloth and has spidery ink writing. It says: THE POUNDS. Under that are six place names from a Bramber that only half exists anymore. The last one is BOATHOUSE. Below that is a row of six numbers with four crossed out. Mrs Okonjo is running the sale. She says the box came from a narrowboat called *The Heron*. It was tied up in the yard for thirty years. She says the man who lived there worked in the old towpath stables.

choices.label: Ask Mrs Okonjo about the boat.
Start at the nearest mark on the compass casing.
Take the card to the canal museum.

nodes.body: Mrs Okonjo has cleared eleven boats in Bramber this year and remembers every one of them, and the paperwork for this one is in a folder in the van. The narrowboat belonged to a man called Harold Vine who died in March, she says, and there is one box of his that has not been priced yet because nobody could decide whether it was junk or something else.

choices.label: Ask to see the unpriced box.
Look at the photographs properly.
Ask to look round the boat itself.

nodes.body: Hold the compass up to the light. The wavy line is the canal. The six marks sit along it in an order that is not the order on the card. The nearest one is fifteen minutes away at the old gauging lock. It is a picnic spot now. A plastic bin stands where the toll-keeper's hut used to be.

choices.label: Go to the gauging lock picnic spot.
Follow the wavy line along the towpath.
Look at the iron footbridge.

nodes.body: The canal museum keeps the history of Bramber on two shelves and a microfilm reader. The reader eats twenty pence coins. Aisha works behind the desk. She has been waiting a long time, most of a year, for someone to come and ask her a question with a date in it.

choices.label: Work the local history shelf.
Get the microfilm reader going.

nodes.body: The unpriced box lives under the van seat and holds a flat cap with a faded red band, two photographs with names written on the back in soft pencil, and a paper wallet of receipts for horse feed, hoof oil and one repaired tow-rope winch. Everything smells faintly of diesel and old wool.

choices.label: Work out who the names belong to.

nodes.body: Two black and white photos. They show men and women standing on a lock-side somewhere in Bramber. There are fourteen people in flat caps, with a heavy horse in the back. On the back in soft pencil are eleven names and the words FIRST SATURDAY. The lock in the picture is not the town lock. It is not anywhere obvious.

nodes.body: Harold Vine led the towpath team for thirty-one years. He kept every receipt he was ever given. He left a narrowboat with one shelf of waterway guides. nodes.body: The story runs on Friday. It has a photo of an empty store and a skip. It is a good piece of writing about something that is already over. Four people write in. They say they would have helped if anyone had asked them on Tuesday.

Eleven walkers set out in the cold. They have one borrowed horn, a copied map, and six brass plates. They stop at all six spots and play badly at each one. More people follow them than anyone thought, and half of those people are under twelve.

Forty people walk the path one Saturday in October. They follow a man who is eighty-four years old. He stops at each brass plate and tells what was there before. At the lock, where there is no plate, everyone stands in a picnic spot and still listens.

Five plates are put back on five walls with the right screws. The sixth plate is cut new in brass by a man on the work estate. He will not take money for it. The plate goes onto the lock wall, in the blank spot that waited for it for twenty-eight years.

The compass goes back into its case. The folded card sits beside it. It lives on a shelf and gets looked at about once a week. It is the only thing in this story that ends up just where it began, but now it means something else entirely.

ending.title: Six Plates Back on Six Walls

nodes.body: Leather goes to the school. Paper to the museum. Photo to the old folks’ home. Plates to the walls. The card goes to the files with a note that tells who found it. It takes three weeks of small, dull tasks. Nothing stays in a bag under a bed.

Two men take the store out onto the grass. They list and photograph everything, then split it into keep and skip. They are paid by the hour and seem oddly keen to help. By the end of the week, the room under the boathouse is swept, dry, and bare.

The skip truck leaves the basin at nine on Friday. In it is a brass horn and four leather cases. A photo is taken of it going from the gate. The paper will not print the photo because there is nothing to say about it.

Three grown-ups each could have stopped it. Nobody told them. Asking on a Wednesday felt like a very, very big deal. But by Monday, when all three said they would have helped, it didn't feel so big anymore.

The last order is wrong. The wheels go back to zero. A trail started in a shoebox in the boat yard. It ran through six walls and sixty years. It ends at a steel door in a cold basin, with a truck booked for the morning.

ending.title: The Trail Ends at a Steel Door
